pos: n. (the proper name and title of the one living and true God; in the Authorized Version rendering Hebrew 'el, 'eloah, 'elōhīm and Greek theos)
etymology: From Old English god, common Germanic (Gothic guþ, Old High German got), of uncertain ultimate root — probably from Proto-Germanic *gudan, a neuter noun meaning “that which is invoked” or “that which is poured to” in libation. The Anglo-Saxon evangelists took a heathen word and put it under the discipline of Scripture, capitalizing it and confining it to the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. In the Authorized Version God renders the Hebrew 'elōhīm (a plural of majesty governing singular verbs) and the Greek theos; LORD in small capitals renders the covenant name YHWH, which is a distinct thing and must not be confused with it.
biblical_def: God is the one living and true God, eternal, infinite, most pure spirit, invisible, without body, parts, or passions, immutable, immense, almighty, every way infinite, most holy, most wise, most free, most absolute, working all things according to the counsel of His own immutable and most righteous will, for His own glory. Scripture never argues for His existence; it opens by assuming it — “In the beginning God created the heaven and the earth” (Gen 1:1). He names Himself to Moses as sheer self-existent being, “I AM THAT I AM” (Exo 3:14), the ground of the doctrine of aseity: He has life in Himself and derives nothing from anything outside Himself. He is one in essence — “Hear, O Israel: The LORD our God is one LORD” (Deu 6:4) — and three in Person: Father, Son, and Holy Ghost, the same in substance, equal in power and glory. He is spirit, and therefore worshipped in spirit and in truth (Joh 4:24), never through image or likeness. The word occurs 4,367 times in the Authorized Version, more than any other substantive in Scripture; it is the subject of the first sentence of the Bible and the last blessing of Revelation. Everything else in this dictionary is defined in relation to Him.
webster_summary: The one living and true God: eternal, self-existent, simple, immutable, almighty, most holy, one in essence and three in Person — Father, Son, and Holy Ghost — the Creator, Preserver, and Governor of all things, and the chief end of man.
webster_full: GOD, n. 1. The Supreme Being; Jehovah; the eternal and infinite spirit, the creator, and the sovereign of the universe. God is a spirit; and they that worship him, must worship him in spirit and in truth. John 4.

2. A false god; a heathen deity; an idol. Fear not the gods of the Amorites. Judges 6. Webster's 1828 entry preserves the distinction the Authorized Version keeps throughout: the word is used absolutely of the true God and derivatively of the idols the nations set in His place.

3. A person or thing exalted to the place of supreme regard; whatever a man makes his ultimate trust. “Whose god is their belly” (Php 3:19). This third sense is not a metaphor loosely used but the biblical definition of idolatry.

The confessional definition stands behind every use of the word in this dictionary. The Second London Baptist Confession (1689) 2.1 reads: “The Lord our God is but one only living and true God; whose subsistence is in and of himself, infinite in being and perfection, whose essence cannot be comprehended by any but himself; a most pure spirit, invisible, without body, parts, or passions, who only hath immortality.”

The name is not a genus into which the God of Scripture is placed as one instance. When the Bible says God, it does not mean a member of the class of deities distinguished by superior attributes; it means the only one there is, beside whom there is no other (Isa 45:5), and every other claimant is by definition an idol.
scriptures: Gen 1:1
In the beginning God created the heaven and the earth.
Exo 3:14
And God said unto Moses, I AM THAT I AM: and he said, Thus shalt thou say unto the children of Israel, I AM hath sent me unto you.
Deu 6:4
Hear, O Israel: The LORD our God is one LORD:
Joh 4:24
God is a Spirit: and they that worship him must worship him in spirit and in truth.
corruption_summary: The modern corruption of the word God is not chiefly atheism but domestication: a warm, agreeable, permissive deity assembled from therapeutic sentiment, who affirms whatever the worshipper already wanted — and, on the academic side, the Open Theist and process denial of the very attributes the word has always carried.
corruption_paragraphs: The reigning American deity has been named accurately by sociologists as Moralistic Therapeutic Deism: a God who wants people to be nice, who wants them to feel good about themselves, who does not need to be particularly involved except when a problem arises, and who takes good people to heaven when they die. Every clause of that is a denial of the God of Scripture — His holiness, His wrath, His providence, His justification of the ungodly by grace alone. The corruption works by subtraction: nothing is formally denied, but sovereignty, holiness, and judgment quietly cease to be mentioned, until the word God retains only the residue that flatters. A congregation can sing about this deity for years without ever once being confronted by the God who says “I AM THAT I AM.”

The academic corruption is bolder. Open Theism (Clark Pinnock, Gregory Boyd, John Sanders) denies exhaustive divine foreknowledge, making God a learner within time; process theology (following Whitehead and Hartshorne) denies immutability and omnipotence outright, reducing God to the most influential participant in a universe He does not govern. Both are departures not merely from Reformed confession but from every historic Christian creed. The Reformed answer is the classical one: God is pure act, without composition, without becoming, without succession of states — and therefore His promises cannot fail, since nothing in Him can change and nothing outside Him can compel Him. A God who might learn something tomorrow is a God whose covenant is a wager.
roots_summary: Hebrew 'elōhīm (plural of majesty, singular verbs), 'el (the Mighty), 'elyōn (Most High), and shadday (Almighty), rendered by Greek theos in the Septuagint and the New Testament; distinguished throughout the Authorized Version from the covenant name YHWH, printed LORD.
roots_lines: 'elōhīm (Hebrew, Strong's H430) — the ordinary Old Testament word for God, morphologically plural but taking singular verbs when it denotes the true God; the grammar is a plural of majesty and fullness, and it stands ready for the fuller Trinitarian revelation of the New Testament without itself proving it.
'el (Hebrew, H410) — the older Semitic root, “mighty, strong”; survives in the great compound names El Shaddai, El Elyon, El Roi, and embedded in Israel, Bethel, Elijah, Daniel.

YHWH (Hebrew, H3068) — the covenant name given at the bush, rendered LORD in small capitals by the Authorized Version following the Septuagint's kyrios. It is a name, not a title, and Exo 3:14 ties it to the verb hayah, to be.

theos (Greek, G2316) — the Septuagint and New Testament rendering of both 'elōhīm and, joined to kyrios, of the covenant name; applied without qualification to the Son (Joh 1:1; Joh 20:28; Tit 2:13; Heb 1:8) and to the Spirit by implication (Act 5:3–4).

1689 London Baptist Confession, chapters 2–3 — the dictionary's confessional standard on the divine essence, the decree, and the Trinity; chapter 2.3 is the Baptist restatement of Nicene orthodoxy, including eternal generation and eternal procession.
usage: The Authorized Version's typography is doing doctrinal work that modern readers routinely miss: God renders 'elōhīm, Lord renders 'adōnay, and LORD in small capitals renders the covenant name. “The LORD our God is one LORD” is not repetition; it is the name and the title set side by side.

That the corpus of this dictionary carried entries for attributes-of-god and city-of-god before it carried one for god is a parable of how theological vocabularies grow — outward from the technical terms, and only late back to the plain words the text actually uses most.

When a man says he does not believe in God, the first pastoral question is which god he means, because the deity most often rejected in modern conversation — capricious, petty, hostile to joy — is one Scripture rejects too.

pos: n. (the human creature made in God's image; also, specifically, the male of the species; in the Authorized Version rendering Hebrew 'adam, 'īsh, 'enōsh, geber and Greek anthrōpos, anēr)
etymology: From Old English mann, common Germanic, originally meaning “human being” without regard to sex; the sex-specific sense (over against wifman, whence woman) grew alongside it and both senses are alive in the Authorized Version. Hebrew 'adam carries the same double duty and is bound by a pun to 'adamah, the ground: the man is the earthling, formed of dust. 'īsh is the male over against 'ishshah, the woman taken out of him (Gen 2:23). Greek anthrōpos is the human being; anēr is the man as male and husband.
biblical_def: Man is the creature God made last on the sixth day, male and female, in His own image and after His likeness, to have dominion over the works of His hands. He is dust and breath together: “the LORD God formed man of the dust of the ground, and breathed into his nostrils the breath of life; and man became a living soul” (Gen 2:7). He is therefore neither a beast nor an angel but a body-soul unity, mortal in his frame and immortal in his soul, made for worship and for work. The image is not a faculty man possesses but a status he bears, and it is not forfeited by the Fall: after Eden, murder is still capital because the image is still there (Gen 9:6). Yet the whole man fell in Adam — mind, will, affections, body — so that by nature he is dead in trespasses and sins and cannot of himself turn to God. Scripture answers this ruin not with a program of improvement but with a second Man: “The first man is of the earth, earthy: the second man is the Lord from heaven” (1Co 15:47). The Psalmist's astonishment — “What is man, that thou art mindful of him?” (Psa 8:4) — is answered finally in the Incarnation, where God took this nature to Himself and did not lay it down.
webster_summary: The human creature, male and female, made in the image of God, formed of the dust and animated by the breath of God; a body-soul unity, fallen in Adam, redeemable only in Christ the second Man.
webster_full: MAN, n. plu. men. [Sax. man, mann; Goth. manna.] 1. Mankind; the human race; the whole species of human beings. And God said, Let us make man in our image. Gen. 1.
2. A male individual of the human race, of adult growth or years. And the rib, which the Lord God had taken from man, made he a woman. Gen. 2.
3. A servant, an attendant, a dependent; one under the authority or in the household of another.

4. Man is used to denote the human nature considered in its weakness and mortality, over against God: “It is better to trust in the Lord than to put confidence in man.” Ps. 118. This is the sense of Isaiah's “Cease ye from man, whose breath is in his nostrils.”

5. In theology, the old man and the new man (Rom 6:6; Eph 4:22–24; Col 3:9–10) name not two persons but the whole man as he stands in Adam and as he stands in Christ — the corrupted nature to be put off and the renewed nature to be put on.
scriptures: Gen 1:27
So God created man in his own image, in the image of God created he him; male and female created he them.
Gen 2:7
And the LORD God formed man of the dust of the ground, and breathed into his nostrils the breath of life; and man became a living soul.
Psa 8:4
What is man, that thou art mindful of him? and the son of man, that thou visitest him?
The first man is of the earth, earthy: the second man is the Lord from heaven.
corruption_summary: Two corruptions run in opposite directions and meet in the same place: naturalism, which makes man an accident of matter with no image to bear, and gender ideology, which detaches the person from the embodied sex God gave him — both denying that Gen 1:27 is a statement about what a human being actually is.
corruption_paragraphs: Philosophical naturalism defines man as a complicated animal, the product of undirected process, whose sense of dignity is an evolutionary artifact. Everything the Bible calls man — image-bearer, worshipper, covenant party, moral agent answerable at a judgment — is on that account a useful fiction. The corruption is rarely announced; it arrives as an assumption in a textbook, and its pastoral fruit is despair, because a creature with no Maker has no ground for the worth he cannot stop believing he has. Scripture's answer is not that man is grander than he thought but that he is dustier and more honored at once: formed of the ground, and crowned with glory and honour (Psa 8:5).

The second corruption grants that man is more than matter and then severs him from his body. Modern gender identity theory holds that the inward sense of self is the real person and the sexed body a contingent circumstance to be brought into line with it. Gen 1:27 forecloses this: God created them male and female, and the Lord Jesus grounded the whole doctrine of marriage on that clause (Mat 19:4). Sex is creational, embodied, and given — not assigned, not chosen, and not a costume. The church owes every person caught in this confusion the full dignity of the image he bears and the full truth about the body he was given; the one without the other is not compassion but abandonment.
roots_summary: Hebrew 'adam (humankind, bound by pun to 'adamah, ground), 'īsh (male, husband), 'enōsh (man in his frailty), geber (the strong man); Greek anthrōpos (human being) and anēr (male, husband).
roots_lines: 'adam (Hebrew, H120) — humankind generically and the first man personally; the wordplay with 'adamah (ground, H127) is the point of Gen 2:7 and of the sentence “dust thou art, and unto dust shalt thou return.”
'īsh (Hebrew, H376) — the male, and by extension the husband; paired with 'ishshah (woman, H802) in Gen 2:23, where the naming establishes the creational order Paul reasons from in 1Co 11:8–9.
'enōsh (Hebrew, H582) — man in his weakness and mortality; the word in Psa 8:4a, which is why the verse is a confession of frailty before it is a celebration of dignity.

anthrōpos (Greek, G444) — human being; the New Testament's word in the Adam-Christ parallels (Rom 5:12–19; 1Co 15:21–22, 45–49), where the whole argument depends on Adam being a historical man and not a symbol.

1689 London Baptist Confession 4.2 and 6.1–3 — man created upright with the law written on his heart, and the whole race falling in Adam as the covenant head, so that original sin is imputed and corruption inherited.
usage: The Authorized Version's generic man is not a slip to be edited out. It renders a Hebrew and Greek usage in which the male name stands for the race — a linguistic pattern that carries the doctrine of headship, and which Rom 5:12 requires in order to argue at all.

“What is man?” is asked three times in Scripture (Job 7:17; Psa 8:4; Psa 144:3) and answered differently each time — a creature too small to be worth God's notice, and yet noticed; the tension resolves only at Bethlehem.

Preachers should mark that Paul calls Christ the second man, not the third or the millionth: in redemptive history there are exactly two men whose acts count for others, and every human being stands under one or the other.

pos: n. (a body of persons constituted as one, especially the covenant nation God takes to Himself; in the Authorized Version rendering Hebrew 'am, gōy, l'ōm and Greek laos, ethnos, dēmos)
etymology: From Old French pople, peuple, from Latin populus, the body of citizens (whence popular, public, republic). Hebrew 'am is the older and warmer word — kinsfolk, the people to whom one belongs, related to a root for paternal kin — and is the standard term for Israel as the LORD's own. Gōy is the nation as a political and ethnic body, and in the plural becomes the Gentiles. The Septuagint fixed the distinction with laos for Israel and ethnē for the nations, and the New Testament writers exploit exactly that distinction when they call the church a laos.
biblical_def: A people, in Scripture, is not an aggregate of individuals but a body constituted by covenant. The word is the load-bearing term of the covenant formula that runs from Exodus to Revelation: “I will take you to me for a people, and I will be to you a God” (Exo 6:7). Israel is a people not by blood alone but by God's choosing — “the LORD thy God hath chosen thee to be a special people unto himself” (Deu 7:6) — and that election is unconditional, resting on His love and His oath rather than on anything in them (Deu 7:7–8). The New Testament does not abolish the category but fills it: Peter applies Israel's own titles to a congregation of Jews and Gentiles together, “a chosen generation, a royal priesthood, an holy nation, a peculiar people” (1Pe 2:9). The church is therefore not a voluntary society of like-minded individuals but the covenant people of God, gathered by effectual call, marked by baptism, fed at the Lord's table, and governed by elders. The formula reaches its consummation when the dwelling of God is with men: “they shall be his people, and God himself shall be with them” (Rev 21:3). The whole Bible is the story of God getting Himself a people.
webster_summary: A body of persons constituted as one — by kinship, by nation, or supremely by covenant; in Scripture, the company God chooses, redeems, and dwells among, first Israel and then the church gathered from every nation.
webster_full: PEOPLE, n. [L. populus.] 1. The body of persons who compose a community, town, city or nation. We speak of the people of a town, the people of a city or district.
2. The vulgar; the mass of illiterate persons, as distinguished from the rulers and the learned.
3. The commonalty, as distinct from men of rank. Myself was stirring ere the break of day, and now the people are assembling.

4. Persons of a particular class; as, the people of a congregation. In Scripture the word takes on its covenantal weight: “Blessed is the nation whose God is the Lord; and the people whom he hath chosen for his own inheritance.” Ps. 33.

5. In the plural, peoples, distinct nations or tribes considered severally — the sense in Rev 7:9, where a multitude stands before the throne out of all nations, and kindreds, and people, and tongues.
scriptures: Exo 6:7
And I will take you to me for a people, and I will be to you a God: and ye shall know that I am the LORD your God, which bringeth you out from under the burdens of the Egyptians.
Deu 7:6
For thou art an holy people unto the LORD thy God: the LORD thy God hath chosen thee to be a special people unto himself, above all people that are upon the face of the earth.
But ye are a chosen generation, a royal priesthood, an holy nation, a peculiar people; that ye should shew forth the praises of him who hath called you out of darkness into his marvellous light:
Rev 21:3

And I heard a great voice out of heaven saying, Behold, the tabernacle of God is with men, and he will dwell with them, and they shall be his people, and God himself shall be with them, and be their God.
corruption_summary: Modern usage dissolves people into a marketing category or a grievance bloc, and modern church practice dissolves it into an audience — congregants without membership, covenant, or discipline, who attend a service the way they attend a concert.
corruption_paragraphs: The word has been thinned into demographics. A people becomes a segment, an audience, a target, a bloc identified by consumption or by group standing, and the question “whose are you?” is replaced by “which category are you in?” Scripture's categories are not these. The biblical people is defined by whose it is: the LORD's portion is His people, Jacob the lot of His inheritance (Deu 32:9). Where identity is built out of grievance-blocs, the resulting solidarity is permanently at war with every other bloc, because it has no common Father and no shared redemption to reconcile it. Gal 3:28 does not erase the nations; it locates them all in one Man.

The corresponding corruption inside the church is congregational anonymity. A crowd that gathers weekly, receives a service, and disperses without membership, oversight, or discipline is not what the New Testament calls a people. The covenant formula assumes a defined body: God knows who is His, and the church is to know who its members are, or it cannot obey Mat 18:17 or Heb 13:17. Recovering the word means recovering church membership as a covenantal act, elders who can name their sheep, and a table fenced by profession and life. A people has a roll; an audience has attendance figures.
roots_summary: Hebrew 'am (kin, the covenant people) over against gōy (nation, in the plural the Gentiles); Greek laos (the covenant people, and in the New Testament the church) over against ethnos (nation); Latin populus behind the English form.
roots_lines: 'am (Hebrew, H5971) — the people as kindred, the body one belongs to; the word in the covenant formula “I will be your God, and ye shall be my people” (Exo 6:7; Lev 26:12; Jer 31:33; Eze 36:28).
gōy (Hebrew, H1471) — the nation as a political-ethnic body; used of Israel in Exo 19:6 (“an holy nation”) but in the plural becomes the standard term for the Gentiles.

laos (Greek, G2992) — the Septuagint's word for Israel, deliberately applied to the church in Act 15:14, Tit 2:14, 1Pe 2:9–10 and Heb 4:9; the transfer of the term is itself an argument about who the church is.
ethnos (Greek, G1484) — nation; the plural is the New Testament's word for the Gentiles, and Mat 28:19 sends the apostles to make disciples of exactly those.

1689 London Baptist Confession 26.1–2 — the catholic church consists of the whole number of the elect, and particular churches consist of visible saints who by their profession and walk are fit to be members; the doctrinal frame for treating a congregation as a people rather than a crowd.
usage: The Authorized Version routinely uses people as a singular collective — “the people is greater and taller than we” (Deu 1:28) — and the grammar carries the theology: a people acts as one, is judged as one, and is redeemed as one.

The covenant formula “I will be their God, and they shall be my people” appears in some form more than twenty times from Genesis to Revelation; tracing it end to end is one of the simplest ways to show a congregation that the Bible is a single book.
Peter stacks four of Israel's titles on a Gentile-majority church in one verse (1Pe 2:9). That is not a decorative allusion; it is a claim about who inherits the promises.

pos: n. (a dwelling; a household or family; a dynasty; the temple as God's house; the church as God's household; in the Authorized Version rendering Hebrew bayith and Greek oikos, oikia)
etymology: From Old English hūs, common Germanic, a dwelling or shelter. Hebrew bayith and Greek oikos both carry the same threefold reach the English word inherited: the building, the family that lives in it, and the line that descends from it. The Hebrew letter beth, second of the alphabet, is itself the pictograph of a house, and the word forms hundreds of place names — Bethel, the house of God; Bethlehem, the house of bread; Bethany; Bethesda. From oikos English derives economy (the law of the house) and ecumenical (of the whole inhabited house).
biblical_def: House in Scripture runs up a ladder of meanings, and the ladder is the doctrine. First it is the dwelling: Noah is told, “Come thou and all thy house into the ark” (Gen 7:1), where the building and the family are one thing. Second it is the household under a head, the unit in which faith is confessed and covenant obedience rendered: “as for me and my house, we will serve the LORD” (Jos 24:15). Joshua does not poll the household; he speaks for it, which is what headship means. Third it is the dynasty: God refuses David's offer to build Him a house and instead builds David one, “thine house and thy kingdom shall be established for ever” (2Sa 7:16) — a promise no son of David fulfilled until One rose who does not die. Fourth it is the temple, the house of God, where His name dwells. And fifth, gathering all the others, it is the church: “the house of God, which is the church of the living God, the pillar and ground of the truth” (1Ti 3:15). Peter completes the figure by making the members themselves the material — lively stones built up a spiritual house (1Pe 2:5). What began as shelter ends as the dwelling of God with men.
webster_summary: A dwelling; the family or household that inhabits it; the dynasty descended from it; the temple as God's dwelling; and, in the New Testament, the church as the household of God built of living stones.
webster_full: HOUSE, n. [Sax. hus.] 1. In a general sense, a building or shed intended or used as a habitation or shelter for animals of any kind; but appropriately, a building or edifice for the habitation of man.
2. A household; a family of ancestors, descendants and kindred; a race of persons from the same stock; a tribe. The Lord hath sworn unto David... of the house of Judah.
3. A body of men assembled in legislative capacity; as the house of lords or commons. The English political sense preserves the older idea of a corporate body treated as one.
4. In Scripture, the temple: “My house shall be called an house of prayer.” Matt. 21. And the church, considered as God's dwelling among men.
5. The grave, the long home; and, figuratively, the body as the soul's tabernacle — “our earthly house of this tabernacle” (2Co 5:1), a house pitched for a journey and struck at its end.
scriptures: Gen 7:1
And the LORD said unto Noah, Come thou and all thy house into the ark; for thee have I seen righteous before me in this generation.

And if it seem evil unto you to serve the LORD, choose you this day whom ye will serve; whether the gods which your fathers served that were on the other side of the flood, or the gods of the Amorites, in whose land ye dwell: but as for me and my house, we will serve the LORD.
And thine house and thy kingdom shall be established for ever before thee: thy throne shall be established for ever.
But if I tarry long, that thou mayest know how thou oughtest to behave thyself in the house of God, which is the church of the living God, the pillar and ground of the truth.
corruption_summary: The household as a governed unit with a head, a table, and a confession has been replaced by the house as a private consumption space — and in the church, the household-of-God image has been traded for the corporation, with the pastor recast as executive and the members as clients.
corruption_paragraphs: The biblical house is a small commonwealth: it has a head accountable to God, a confession spoken on its behalf, work and worship under one roof, and children catechized within it (Deu 6:6–9; Eph 6:4). What replaced it is a residence — a place where individuals who share an address sleep, charge devices, and depart to separate lives. The change is not merely sociological; it dismantles the unit through which Scripture ordinarily works. Joshua's “as for me and my house” is unintelligible where no one may speak for anyone. Recovering family worship, the family table, and the father's duty to teach is not nostalgia for an era; it is obedience to a standing command.

The parallel corruption runs in the church. When 1Ti 3:15 calls the church God's house, it sets Paul's whole instruction about elders and deacons in a domestic frame — which is precisely why an elder who cannot rule his own house is disqualified from the greater one (1Ti 3:4–5). The corporate model severs that logic: it measures leadership by attendance, revenue, and brand, and it treats members as a customer base whose preferences set the agenda. A household is governed by a father; a corporation is steered by a market. The regulative principle and plural eldership are the practical guards on this, because both put the house under its Owner rather than its occupants.
roots_summary: Hebrew bayith (house, household, dynasty, temple) and its place-name compounds Beth-el, Beth-lehem, Beth-any; Greek oikos and oikia, source of oikonomia (stewardship, economy) and oikodomē (edification, building up).
roots_lines: bayith (Hebrew, H1004) — house, household, dynasty, temple; the pun at the centre of 2Sa 7, where David offers to build the LORD a bayith and is told the LORD will build him one instead.

beth- (Hebrew prefix) — the construct form behind Bethel (house of God, Gen 28:17–19), Bethlehem (house of bread), Bethesda, Bethany; the second letter of the alphabet is itself the pictograph of a house.
oikos (Greek, G3624) — house and household; the word in the household baptisms of Act 16:15 and Act 16:33, and in Heb 3:6, “whose house are we, if we hold fast the confidence.”
oikonomia (Greek, G3622) — the law or management of a house, whence economy and stewardship; Paul calls his apostleship a dispensation, that is, a stewardship of God's house (1Co 9:17; Eph 3:2).
1689 London Baptist Confession 26.2 and chapter 22 — the particular church as the visible household of God, and family worship as a duty binding on every household head, “in private families daily.”
usage: “As for me and my house” is quoted constantly and understood rarely: Joshua is exercising headship, publicly binding a household to the LORD, in a speech whose whole point is that neutrality is not on the ballot.
The Hebrew pun in 2Sa 7 — David will not build the house, God will build his — is the hinge of the Davidic covenant and the reason Matthew opens his Gospel with a genealogy.
Preaching 1Ti 3:15 without its domestic frame flattens it into a slogan about doctrine. Paul's point is behavioural: this is how a man conducts himself inside his Father's house.

pos: n. (ground, territory, country; especially the land of promise given to Abraham's seed and held of the LORD as its Owner; in the Authorized Version rendering Hebrew 'erets, 'adamah and Greek gē, chōra)
etymology: From Old English land, common Germanic, ground or defined territory. Hebrew 'erets is the great word of the Old Testament for both earth and land — context alone decides whether the whole globe or one country is meant — while 'adamah is the tilled soil, the arable ground from which man was taken and to which he returns. Greek gē covers the same range. English keeps a trace of the covenant sense in landed, landlord, and inheritance language generally.
biblical_def: Land is the second great promise of the Abrahamic covenant, standing beside seed and blessing: “Get thee out of thy country... unto a land that I will shew thee” (Gen 12:1). Canaan is given, but never sold outright, because the title never leaves God's hands: “The land shall not be sold for ever: for the land is mine; for ye are strangers and sojourners with me” (Lev 25:23). Israel holds it as a tenant, which is the ground of the whole jubilee legislation, of the sabbath years for the soil, and of the prophets' fury at those who join field to field. The land is also morally responsive: it is defiled by bloodshed and idolatry and vomits out its inhabitants (Lev 18:25–28), and it is watched continually by its Owner — “the eyes of the LORD thy God are always upon it” (Deu 11:12). Exile is therefore not a political accident but a covenant sanction. The New Testament does not discard the promise; it enlarges it. Abraham himself lived in the land of promise as in a strange country (Heb 11:9), looking past it for a city with foundations, and Paul says the promise to Abraham was that he should be the heir of the world (Rom 4:13). The meek inherit the earth, and the land promise terminates on a renewed creation.
webster_summary: Ground or territory; in Scripture, chiefly the land of promise given to Abraham's seed and held as tenants of the LORD who owns it — a possession forfeited by covenant unfaithfulness and enlarged in Christ to the whole renewed earth.
webster_full: LAND, n. [Sax. land, lond.] 1. Earth, or the solid matter which constitutes the fixed part of the surface of the globe, in distinction from the sea or other waters.
2. Any portion of the solid, superficial part of the globe, whether a kingdom or country, or a particular region. The united provinces of Holland are a rich land.
3. Ground; soil, or the superficial part of the earth in respect to its nature or quality; as good land; poor land.
4. Real estate; a legal freehold. In Scripture the term carries the further sense of a covenant grant: Israel holds Canaan of the Lord, on terms, and may be evicted for breach of them.

5. The land of the living (Psa 27:13) — the sphere of present life under the sun, over against the grave; and by contrast the better country, that is, an heavenly, which the patriarchs desired (Heb 11:16).
scriptures: Gen 12:1
Now the LORD had said unto Abram, Get thee out of thy country, and from thy kindred, and from thy father's house, unto a land that I will shew thee:
The land shall not be sold for ever: for the land is mine; for ye are strangers and sojourners with me.
A land which the LORD thy God careth for: the eyes of the LORD thy God are always upon it, from the beginning of the year even unto the end of the year.
Heb 11:9
By faith he sojourned in the land of promise, as in a strange country, dwelling in tabernacles with Isaac and Jacob, the heirs with him of the same promise:
corruption_summary: Two errors flank the doctrine: dispensational premillennialism, which detaches a national land promise from its fulfilment in Christ and reads modern geopolitics as prophecy; and absolute private property, which forgets Lev 25:23 and treats an estate as a possession owed to no one.
corruption_paragraphs: Dispensational premillennialism, a nineteenth-century system originating with J. N. Darby and popularized by the Scofield Reference Bible, severs Israel from the church and holds that the land promise awaits a literal national fulfilment in a future earthly millennium. No Reformation confession contains this scheme, and the New Testament reads the promise otherwise: Paul says the promise to Abraham was that he should be heir of the world (Rom 4:13), Hebrews says the patriarchs were looking past Canaan to a city with foundations (Heb 11:10, 16), and Joshua flatly records that the LORD gave Israel all the land He sware to their fathers (Jos 21:43–45). The pastoral damage of the corruption is a church reading newspapers for prophecy and treating a modern state's borders as a doctrine.

The opposite error is nearer home. Where Scripture makes every landholder a tenant — “the land is mine” — modern property theory makes him an absolute owner accountable to no one. The jubilee, the sabbath year, the gleaning laws, the redemption of a kinsman's field: every one of them presupposes that possession is stewardship and that the poor have a claim the owner may not simply refuse. This is not a socialist reading; the eighth commandment is intact and Naboth's vineyard is inviolable precisely because it is a covenant inheritance. It is the correction that ownership is real and derivative at once, and that the Owner audits.
roots_summary: Hebrew 'erets (land and earth alike) and 'adamah (tilled soil, the ground man was taken from); Greek gē and chōra; bound in the Old Testament to nachalah (inheritance) and yōbel (jubilee).
roots_lines: 'erets (Hebrew, H776) — earth, land, country; the same word opens Genesis (“the heaven and the earth”) and names Canaan, so the land promise is always audibly a down payment on the whole.
'adamah (Hebrew, H127) — the arable ground, cursed for man's sake in Gen 3:17 and the source of the man's own name; the soil is a party to the Fall and to the restoration.
nachalah (Hebrew, H5159) — inheritance, the allotted portion; the tribal allotments of Joshua 13–21 are nachalah, and the word carries over to the believer's inheritance in 1Pe 1:4.
yōbel (Hebrew, H3104) — the jubilee, the fiftieth year in which every man returned to his possession (Lev 25:10); the mechanism by which the LORD's ownership was made annual and visible.

1689 London Baptist Confession 7 and 8.6 — the covenant of grace administered under both testaments with the same substance, so that the land promise is not a separate track for a separate people but a shadow of the inheritance secured in Christ.
usage: Because Hebrew 'erets means both land and earth, Mat 5:5 (“the meek... shall inherit the earth”) is quoting Psa 37:11 in a way that deliberately opens the smaller promise onto the larger one.
The sabbath years were not agricultural theory. 2Ch 36:21 says the exile lasted seventy years so the land could enjoy the sabbaths Israel had refused it — a debt collected on the soil's behalf.
Naboth's refusal to sell (1Ki 21:3) is not stubbornness but obedience to Lev 25:23; Ahab's inability to understand that refusal is the measure of how far the house of Omri had left the covenant.

pos: n. (the created globe and all that fills it; the dry land as distinct from the sea; the present order as distinct from heaven; in the Authorized Version rendering Hebrew 'erets, 'adamah, tebel and Greek gē, oikoumenē)
etymology: From Old English eorþe, common Germanic, ground or soil, and by extension the whole world. Hebrew 'erets is the word of Gen 1:1, embracing the globe, the dry land, and any particular country; tebel is the habitable, ordered world, and appears chiefly in poetry. Greek gē covers the same ground and yields English geography and geology; oikoumenē is the inhabited earth, and yields ecumenical. The Authorized Version's earth is thus never a synonym for nature in the modern abstract sense; it is always a made thing with an Owner.
biblical_def: The earth is the creation of God, made out of nothing in the beginning (Gen 1:1), declared very good, cursed for man's sake, upheld by the word of His power, and destined for renewal rather than annihilation. Its first and governing fact is ownership: “The earth is the LORD'S, and the fulness thereof” (Psa 24:1) — a verse Paul twice quotes to settle a practical question of conscience (1Co 10:26, 28). It is not divine and not eternal. It is the footstool of the throne, so that no temple built on it can contain its Maker: “The heaven is my throne, and the earth is my footstool” (Isa 66:1). Man was set over it under God with a real commission to subdue and to keep, which makes dominion a stewardship rather than a licence. The earth groans under the curse and waits for the manifestation of the sons of God (Rom 8:19–22), and the Lord Jesus promises it as an inheritance to the meek (Mat 5:5) — not as a consolation for losing it now but as the actual endowment of the humble. The Christian hope is therefore not escape from the earth into a disembodied heaven but a new heavens and a new earth wherein dwelleth righteousness.
webster_summary: The globe God created out of nothing, together with all that fills it — His possession, man's stewardship, the theatre of redemption, cursed for man's sake and destined to be renewed rather than abolished.
webster_full: EARTH, n. [Sax. eorth, eorthe.] 1. Earth, in its primary sense, signifies the particles which compose the mass of the globe, but more particularly the particles which form the fine soft mold on the surface.
2. The terraqueous globe which we inhabit. The earth is nearly spherical, a little flattened at the poles.
3. The world, as opposed to other scenes of existence. God hath given the earth to the children of men.
4. The inhabitants of the globe. The whole earth was of one language. Gen. 11. This is the sense of “let all the earth keep silence before him” (Hab 2:20).

5. In Scripture, the present order under the curse, over against the heavens — and, in prophecy, the object of renewal: “For, behold, I create new heavens and a new earth” (Isa 65:17), which Peter and John take up as the Christian's settled expectation.
scriptures: Gen 1:1
In the beginning God created the heaven and the earth.
Psa 24:1
The earth is the LORD'S, and the fulness thereof; the world, and they that dwell therein.
Isa 66:1
Thus saith the LORD, The heaven is my throne, and the earth is my footstool... where is the house that ye build unto me? and where is the place of my rest?
Mat 5:5
Blessed are the meek: for they shall inherit the earth.
corruption_summary: The earth is corrupted in two directions at once: divinized as Gaia or Mother Earth by neo-pagan environmentalism, and despised by an over-spiritualized evangelicalism that expects it to be burned up and therefore treats stewardship as wasted labour.
corruption_paragraphs: Modern deep ecology and the Gaia hypothesis promote the earth from creature to organism to deity, and the language follows: Mother Earth, the planet as a self-regulating being with interests of its own that man violates by existing. This is not conservation; it is the exchange of the truth of God for a lie, worshipping and serving the creature more than the Creator (Rom 1:25). The biblical correction is exact and unsentimental. The earth is the LORD'S, not its own; man is set over it by commission (Gen 1:28) and answerable for how he treats it; and the goodness of the creation is real precisely because it is derived. A creation that is divine cannot be stewarded, only appeased.

The opposite error is quieter and more common in conservative churches: since the earth is passing away, why paint the woodwork? This mistakes the biblical picture. Rom 8:21 says the creation itself shall be delivered from the bondage of corruption, and Isa 65:17 and Rev 21:1 announce a new heavens and a new earth — renewal, not replacement of the material by the immaterial. The bodily resurrection settles the matter: a raised body needs a real world to live in. Christians who expect a renewed earth have every reason to plant orchards, keep fields, build well, and leave a place better than they found it, without ever confusing the gift with the Giver.
roots_summary: Hebrew 'erets (earth, land, country), 'adamah (soil), tebel (the habitable world); Greek gē (earth, whence geology) and oikoumenē (the inhabited earth, whence ecumenical).
roots_lines: 'erets (Hebrew, H776) — the word of Gen 1:1; its double range (globe and country) is why the land promise to Abraham always carries an echo of the whole creation.
tebel (Hebrew, H8398) — the world as ordered and habitable, chiefly poetic; “the world, and they that dwell therein” in Psa 24:1 renders it, pairing the fertile order with the bare ground.
gē (Greek, G1093) — earth; the Septuagint's rendering of 'erets, and the word in Mat 5:5, so that the Beatitude is heard in Greek as a direct quotation of Psa 37:11.
oikoumenē (Greek, G3625) — the inhabited earth, the term behind Luk 2:1 (“all the world should be taxed”) and Act 17:31 (God will judge the world in righteousness).

1689 London Baptist Confession 4.1 — God created the world and all things therein in the space of six days, and all very good; the confessional ground for treating the material creation as genuinely and permanently good.
usage: Psa 24:1 is Paul's answer to a scruple about meat in the marketplace (1Co 10:26). The doctrine of creation is not an abstraction in the New Testament; it settles what a Christian may eat.
“Heaven and earth” functions in Hebrew as a merism — the two poles standing for everything between — which is why Gen 1:1 is a claim about the whole of what exists, not the first item in a list.
The Beatitude promises the earth to the meek, which is the exact reverse of every observable political fact and is therefore a statement about the age to come rather than a proverb about temperament.

pos: n. (a walled and settled community; in Scripture the ambivalent institution founded by Cain, chosen by God at Jerusalem, judged at Babylon, and consummated as the new Jerusalem; rendering Hebrew 'īr, qiryah and Greek polis)
etymology: From Old French cite, from Latin civitas, the body of citizens (from civis, citizen) — originally the community rather than its buildings, which Latin called urbs. Hebrew 'īr denotes a permanent settlement, usually walled, of any size; qiryah is its poetic partner. Greek polis gives English politics, policy, metropolis, and stands behind politeuma (Php 3:20), the commonwealth or citizenship believers are said to have in heaven.
biblical_def: The city enters Scripture under a shadow: the first builder is Cain, a fugitive who founds a settlement and names it after his son (Gen 4:17), and the first great civic project is Babel, undertaken so that its builders might make themselves a name (Gen 11:4). The city is thus the classic form of man's attempt at security and glory apart from God, and Babylon carries that meaning through the prophets to Revelation. Yet God does not abandon the form; He claims it. He chooses Jerusalem, sets His name there, and the Psalter sings of “the city of God, the holy place of the tabernacles of the most High” (Psa 46:4). The decisive contrast is drawn in Hebrews: Abraham dwelt in tents because “he looked for a city which hath foundations, whose builder and maker is God” (Heb 11:10). Every earthly city, including Jerusalem, is provisional — “here have we no continuing city” (Heb 13:14). The Bible therefore ends where it could not have begun: with a city that no man built, descending out of heaven from God (Rev 21:2). What Cain attempted and Babel parodied, God grants as a gift.
webster_summary: A walled and settled community; in Scripture both the monument of human self-security — Cain's foundation, Babel, Babylon — and the form God claims for Himself at Jerusalem and consummates in the new Jerusalem that comes down from heaven.
webster_full: CITY, n. [L. civitas.] 1. In a general sense, a large town; a large number of houses and inhabitants, established in one place.
2. In a more appropriate sense, a corporate town; a town or collective body of inhabitants, incorporated and governed by particular officers.
3. The collective body of citizens; the community. The whole city went out to meet him.

4. In Scripture, the cities of refuge (Num 35) — six Levitical towns to which the manslayer might flee from the avenger of blood and live, an institution the Reformed tradition has always read as a type of refuge in Christ.
5. The heavenly city; the New Jerusalem; the settled and permanent commonwealth of the redeemed, over against the tents and lodgings of the present pilgrimage.
scriptures: Gen 4:17
And Cain knew his wife; and she conceived, and bare Enoch: and he builded a city, and called the name of the city, after the name of his son, Enoch.
Gen 11:4
And they said, Go to, let us build us a city and a tower, whose top may reach unto heaven; and let us make us a name, lest we be scattered abroad upon the face of the whole earth.
For he looked for a city which hath foundations, whose builder and maker is God.
Rev 21:2
And I John saw the holy city, new Jerusalem, coming down from God out of heaven, prepared as a bride adorned for her husband.
corruption_summary: The city is flattened either into a moral villain — the place Christians flee — or into an idol of progress and belonging that quietly repeats Babel's project of making a name; Scripture does neither, holding both the judgment and the promise.
corruption_paragraphs: One corruption treats the city as inherently corrupt and the countryside as inherently pure, so that faithfulness means withdrawal. Scripture will not support it. Jonah is sent to Nineveh, Jeremiah tells the exiles to seek the peace of the city where they are captive (Jer 29:7), Paul plants churches in the great cities of the empire by deliberate strategy, and the last chapter of the Bible is urban. The retreat instinct also has a practical cost: it abandons the places where the most image-bearers are concentrated and where the church's witness is most visible.

The opposite corruption is Babel restored. The modern city is regularly presented as the engine of human progress, the place where identity is discovered and the collective project is advanced — let us make us a name. Every generation has a version of this, and every version ends in the same confusion, because a community organized around its own glory has no principle of unity that outlasts its success. The believer's posture toward the city is neither flight nor worship but citizenship held lightly: he seeks the welfare of the city he lives in while confessing that his commonwealth is in heaven and that here he has no continuing city.
roots_summary: Hebrew 'īr (settlement, walled town) and qiryah (its poetic partner, embedded in Kirjath-jearim); Greek polis, whence politeuma (commonwealth, Php 3:20) and English politics; Latin civitas behind the English form.
roots_lines: 'īr (Hebrew, H5892) — the ordinary word for a settlement, occurring over a thousand times; it makes no distinction of size, so a fortified village and Jerusalem alike are cities.
qiryah (Hebrew, H7151) — town, poetic; visible in the place names Kirjath-jearim and Kirjath-arba, and in Isaiah's “the faithful city become an harlot” oracle vocabulary.
polis (Greek, G4172) — city; the word in Mat 5:14 (“a city that is set on an hill cannot be hid”) and throughout Hebrews and Revelation for the heavenly city.
politeuma (Greek, G4175) — commonwealth or citizenship; Php 3:20 tells the Philippians, citizens of a Roman colony proud of its status, that their true colony is in heaven.

Augustine, De Civitate Dei (AD 413–426) — the two-cities framework, the earthly city built by love of self to the contempt of God and the city of God built by love of God to the contempt of self; the fountainhead of Reformed reflection on civil order.
usage: That Cain builds the first city and Babel the first tower does not make architecture sinful. Both narratives fault the motive — security and a name apart from God — and the same builder's craft is later commanded for the tabernacle and the temple.
Hebrews sets tents against foundations: Abraham's whole life in Canaan was a refusal to settle, because the land he had been given was not yet the city he was promised.

The new Jerusalem descends. It is not raised. Every attempt to build the heavenly city upward from the earth — whether at Babel or in a political programme — is working against the direction of the promise.

pos: n. (a road or path; a manner of life; the course God appoints; the earliest name for the Christian religion; rendering Hebrew derek, 'ōrach and Greek hodos)
etymology: From Old English weg, common Germanic, a road or course of travel; cognate with Latin via and with the verb to weigh in the older sense of carrying. Hebrew derek is built on a root meaning to tread, so the word literally names the track worn by feet — and the moral sense (a man's way, his habitual course) is the same word without change. Greek hodos is the road, and the compound methodos gives English method, a following-after along a road. Every biblical language uses the same word for the path underfoot and the life lived, and the metaphor is never dead.
biblical_def: Way in Scripture is the standard figure for the whole moral shape of a life, and the Bible knows only two of them. The first Psalm sets them side by side and ends with the LORD's knowledge of one and the perishing of the other: “the LORD knoweth the way of the righteous: but the way of the ungodly shall perish” (Psa 1:6). Proverbs adds the warning that the difference is not obvious to the man walking it — “There is a way which seemeth right unto a man, but the end thereof are the ways of death” (Pro 14:12) — which is why the way must be revealed and not merely felt out. Isaiah promises a highway so plainly marked that the simple cannot lose it: “it shall be called The way of holiness” (Isa 35:8). The figure then collapses into a Person. The Lord Jesus does not say He teaches the way or shows it; He says “I am the way, the truth, and the life: no man cometh unto the Father, but by me” (Joh 14:6). Accordingly the earliest name for the Christian religion in Acts is simply the Way (Act 9:2; 19:9, 23; 24:14, 22) — not a doctrine to be held only, but a road to be walked.
webster_summary: A road or path; by extension the course and manner of a life; in Scripture the two ways of righteousness and destruction, the way of holiness Isaiah foretold, Christ Himself as the only way to the Father, and the Way as the first name of the Christian religion.
webster_full: WAY, n. [Sax. weg.] 1. Literally, a passing; hence, a passage; the place of passing; hence, a road of any kind; a highway; a private road; a lane; a street.
2. Length of space; as a great way; a little way.
3. Course; direction of motion or travel. Which way did he go?
4. Manner of doing any thing; method; means; as, this is the way to be happy. In Scripture, the moral course of a life: “Teach me thy way, O Lord; I will walk in thy truth.” Ps. 86.

5. In Scripture, the ways of God are His providential dealings and His revealed precepts alike — “my ways [are] higher than your ways” (Isa 55:9) speaks of the former, “shew me thy ways, O LORD” (Psa 25:4) of the latter, and the two are never in conflict.
scriptures: Psa 1:6
For the LORD knoweth the way of the righteous: but the way of the ungodly shall perish.
There is a way which seemeth right unto a man, but the end thereof are the ways of death.
Isa 35:8

And an highway shall be there, and a way, and it shall be called The way of holiness; the unclean shall not pass over it; but it shall be for those: the wayfaring men, though fools, shall not err therein.
Joh 14:6
Jesus saith unto him, I am the way, the truth, and the life: no man cometh unto the Father, but by me.
corruption_summary: Religious pluralism recasts Joh 14:6 as one community's testimony rather than a universal claim, teaching that the ways are many and converge; and inside the church, “my walk” is reduced to a private inward experience with no defined road, no destination, and no obedience.
corruption_paragraphs: The pluralist correction of Joh 14:6 is now standard in mainline preaching and in progressive evangelicalism: Jesus is a way, or the way for Christians, and the several religions are so many roads up one mountain. The verse itself forbids the reading, and its second clause exists precisely to close the exit — no man cometh unto the Father, but by me. Peter says the same thing without metaphor (Act 4:12), and Paul stakes the entire mission on it: how shall they hear without a preacher? If the ways converged, the apostolic church wasted its blood. The exclusivity is not the church's arrogance; it is the confession that if a road had already run to the Father, the cross was a needless cruelty.

The domestic corruption is softer. “My walk with the Lord” has drifted into a term for interior mood — how one is feeling about God this month — detached from the commandments, the ordinances, the assembly, and any measurable direction. Scripture's figure is stubbornly external: a way has a surface underfoot, a direction, other travellers on it, and an end. Psalm 119 asks God to teach, incline, order, and quicken the psalmist's way, and every one of those requests is about what he will actually do. The recovery is plain: walk in the commandments, in the light, in love, in newness of life — all of them Pauline imperatives with feet in them.
roots_summary: Hebrew derek (from a root meaning to tread — a trodden path, and so a manner of life) and 'ōrach (a track); Greek hodos (road, whence method), the term Acts uses absolutely for the Christian religion.
roots_lines: derek (Hebrew, H1870) — road, journey, manner of life; some seven hundred occurrences, and the same word carries the literal and moral senses without any shift, which is why Hebrew ethics is habitually described in travel language.
'ōrach (Hebrew, H734) — path, track; the poetic partner of derek, as in Psa 119:104 and the parallelism of Pro 4:18, “the path of the just is as the shining light.”

halak (Hebrew, H1980) — to walk; the verb that supplies the noun's force, and the root of later Jewish halakhah, the rule for walking; the New Testament's peripateō carries the same Hebrew idiom into Greek.
hodos (Greek, G3598) — road, way; used absolutely for the Christian religion at Act 9:2, 19:9, 19:23, 24:14 and 24:22, an idiom that presupposes Isaiah's highway of holiness.

The Two Ways — a teaching form running from Deu 30:15–19 and Psalm 1 through Mat 7:13–14 to the opening of the Didache; the oldest catechetical structure in Christian instruction and the frame for every Puritan treatise on the Christian walk.
usage: The Hebrew word for a moral course is the same word used for a dirt track. Biblical ethics is therefore never abstract: a man's way is where his feet have actually gone, and it can be read by anyone who follows the prints.
Acts calls the church the Way five times before Christian appears once as an outsiders' nickname (Act 11:26). The self-designation the first believers used described a road they were on.
Pro 14:12 is repeated verbatim at Pro 16:25 — a doubling in Hebrew idiom that marks the warning as fixed and certain, not a passing observation.

pos: n. (animate existence, natural and spiritual; the vitality God alone possesses in Himself and gives to His creatures; rendering Hebrew chayyim, nephesh and Greek zōē, psychē, bios)
etymology: From Old English līf, common Germanic, related to to live and to leave in the sense of remaining. Hebrew chayyim is plural in form — lives — and takes singular agreement, a plural of abundance suggesting fullness rather than number. Greek distinguishes what English cannot: bios is the life one lives, its span and means (whence biography, biology); psychē is the animating soul-life a man may lose or save; zōē is life as principle and gift, the word John uses for what is in the Son.
biblical_def: Life belongs to God alone underivatively; every other life is loan and gift. Man receives it by a direct divine act: “the LORD God formed man of the dust of the ground, and breathed into his nostrils the breath of life; and man became a living soul” (Gen 2:7). Because life is given, it is owed — which grounds the sixth commandment, the sanctity of the unborn, and the blood-prohibition of Gen 9. Natural life is real but brief and unpossessable: “What is your life? It is even a vapour, that appeareth for a little time, and then vanisheth away” (Jas 4:14). Scripture then uses the word for a second and higher thing. Spiritual life is not the enhancement of natural life but its resurrection: men dead in trespasses and sins are quickened (Eph 2:1–5), and this life is located wholly in the Son — “In him was life; and the life was the light of men” (Joh 1:4). Christ came that His sheep “might have life, and that they might have it more abundantly” (Joh 10:10), a promise about the quality and permanence of the life given, not about circumstances. Eternal life begins now by faith, is preserved by the perseverance God works in His own, and is consummated in the resurrection of the body.
webster_summary: Animate existence — underived in God, given to His creatures, brief and unpossessable in nature, and given again in Christ as spiritual and eternal life that begins in regeneration and ends in the resurrection of the body.
webster_full: LIFE, n. plu. lives. 1. In a general sense, that state of animals and plants, or of an organized being, in which its natural functions and motions are performed, or in which its organs are capable of performing their functions.
2. In animals, animation; vitality; and in man, that state of being in which the soul and body are united.
3. The present state of existence; the time from birth to death. The life of man seldom exceeds seventy years.
4. Manner of living; conduct; deportment, in regard to morals. I will teach my family to lead good lives.

5. Eternal happiness in heaven; the spiritual state and endless felicity of the redeemed. This is life eternal, that they might know thee the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom thou hast sent. John 17. Also, the animating principle itself: Christ “who is our life” (Col 3:4).
scriptures: Gen 2:7
And the LORD God formed man of the dust of the ground, and breathed into his nostrils the breath of life; and man became a living soul.
Joh 1:4
In him was life; and the life was the light of men.
The thief cometh not, but for to steal, and to kill, and to destroy: I am come that they might have life, and that they might have it more abundantly.
Jas 4:14
Whereas ye know not what shall be on the morrow. For what is your life? It is even a vapour, that appeareth for a little time, and then vanisheth away.
corruption_summary: Joh 10:10 has been detached from its shepherd-and-sheep setting and made the proof text of the prosperity gospel and of self-actualization — abundant life recast as health, wealth, and personal flourishing — while the culture severs the sanctity of life from its Giver and makes it a matter of quality and consent.
corruption_paragraphs: “Life more abundantly” is spoken in the middle of a discourse about a shepherd who lays down His life for the sheep, and the very next verse says so. Wrenched out of it, the sentence has become the banner of the prosperity gospel — abundance as material increase and unbroken health — and of the softer self-actualization preaching that promises the listener his best life now. Both are refuted by the apostles' own lives, which were abundant in the sense John means and destitute in the sense the corruption means. The abundance in view is the quality of the life given: eternal, indestructible, life shared with the Son. Paul had it in a prison cell while writing about rejoicing.

The second corruption is the culture's. Where life is a possession rather than a trust, its worth is measured by projected quality and by the consent of the one holding it, and the weakest lose their claim first: the unborn, the disabled, the aged, the dying. The biblical ground is entirely different. Life is God's to give and God's to take, man is made in His image, and the shedding of innocent blood is therefore an offence against the Maker rather than a private calculation (Gen 9:6). The same doctrine that forbids the taking also commands the caring — the widow, the orphan, the stranger, the afflicted — and a church that defends the unborn while ignoring the aged has only half received it.
roots_summary: Hebrew chayyim (life, plural of abundance) and nephesh (living soul, breathing creature); Greek zōē (life as principle and gift), psychē (soul-life), and bios (the lived span and its means).
roots_lines: chayyim (Hebrew, H2416) — life; plural in form with singular agreement, a plural of fullness; it names the tree of life in Gen 2:9 and the book of life in Psa 69:28.
nephesh (Hebrew, H5315) — soul, living creature, breathing thing; Gen 2:7 says man became a living nephesh, so a man does not have a soul as one item among others but is one.
zōē (Greek, G2222) — life as principle and gift; John's word, occurring some thirty-six times in his Gospel, always of the life that is in the Son and given by Him.
psychē (Greek, G5590) — soul, the animating life; the word in Mat 16:25–26, where losing and saving the same psychē is the whole point of the paradox.

1689 London Baptist Confession 11.1 and 17.1 — justification and the perseverance of the saints; the confessional guarantee that the life given in regeneration cannot be finally lost, since it is Christ's life communicated and not the believer's achievement.
usage: Greek separates bios, psychē, and zōē where English has one word. Preachers reading Joh 10:10 should say plainly which is promised: it is zōē, and no promise about bios — the span or its means — is being made.

James's vapour is not pessimism. It is the premise of an argument about presumption in business plans, and its conclusion is “ye ought to say, If the Lord will” — a doctrine of providence applied to a calendar.

Because Gen 2:7 says man became a living soul rather than received one, the Hebrew resists any scheme that treats the body as a container the real person occupies temporarily — which is why the hope is resurrection rather than escape.

pos: adj. and n. (conformed to the character and will of God; beneficial, upright, excellent; rendering Hebrew tōb and Greek agathos, kalos)
etymology: From Old English gōd, common Germanic, fitting or suitable — the underlying idea being a thing answering to its purpose. English God and good are not etymologically related, a coincidence of spelling only, though the theology binds them tightly enough. Hebrew tōb covers moral goodness, beauty, pleasantness, and practical usefulness in one word, which is why Gen 1 can pronounce the creation good without distinguishing the aesthetic from the ethical. Greek divides the ground: agathos is good in nature and effect, kalos good as beautiful, noble, and fit to be seen.
biblical_def: Good is not an independent standard by which God may be measured; it is a description of what God is, and derivatively of what conforms to Him. Creation's goodness is a verdict He pronounces: “God saw every thing that he had made, and, behold, it was very good” (Gen 1:31). Matter, sex, food, work, and the body are therefore good by divine declaration, and every asceticism that treats them as inherently defiling is corrected at the first page. The Lord Jesus fixes the term's ultimate reference in a single sentence to a man who used it flatteringly: “Why callest thou me good? there is none good but one, that is, God” (Mar 10:18) — not a denial of His own deity but a refusal to let the word float free of it. What God requires of man is likewise not obscure: “He hath shewed thee, O man, what is good” (Mic 6:8), and the content is justice, mercy, and humble walking. And because God is good, He is trustworthy in the dark: “O taste and see that the LORD is good” (Psa 34:8) is an invitation to experiment on His character, and Rom 8:28 extends the verdict over everything that happens to those who love Him. Good works follow salvation as its fruit and never precede it as its price (Eph 2:8–10).
webster_summary: Conformed to the character and will of God; in Scripture the verdict God pronounces on His creation, the description of His own nature, the summary of what He requires of man, and the fruit — never the ground — of salvation.
webster_full: GOOD, a. 1. Valid; legally firm; not weak or defective; having strength adequate to its support; as a good title.
2. Valuable; useful; not bad, hurtful or pernicious; as, good fruit; a good tree.
3. Conformable to the moral law; virtuous; applied to actions. In this sense it is equivalent to right.
4. Complete or sufficiently perfect in its kind; having the physical qualities best adapted to its design and use; as good timber; a good soil.

5. GOOD, n. That which contributes to diminish or remove pain, or to increase happiness or prosperity; benefit; advantage. In theology, the chief good is God Himself, in whose enjoyment the creature's blessedness consists — the summum bonum of the older divines.
scriptures: Gen 1:31
And God saw every thing that he had made, and, behold, it was very good. And the evening and the morning were the sixth day.
Psa 34:8
O taste and see that the LORD is good: blessed is the man that trusteth in him.
Mic 6:8
He hath shewed thee, O man, what is good; and what doth the LORD require of thee, but to do justly, and to love mercy, and to walk humbly with thy God?
And Jesus said unto him, Why callest thou me good? there is none good but one, that is, God.
corruption_summary: Moral relativism detaches good from God and reduces it to preference or social consensus, so that the word survives while its standard is gone; and Mic 6:8 is regularly quoted as a programme of social action with its third clause — walking humbly with thy God — quietly dropped.
corruption_paragraphs: Once good is severed from God it can only mean what a person or a culture approves, and the word becomes a container for whatever is currently applauded. The Lord Jesus refused this move in advance: there is none good but one, that is, God. Goodness is not a standard external to Him that He happens to meet, nor an arbitrary decree He might have issued otherwise; it is His nature, and the moral law is its published expression. This is why a society can retain the vocabulary of good and evil long after it has abandoned any means of adjudicating between them, and why appeals to decency grow shriller as the ground for them erodes.

The second corruption is a selective quotation. Mic 6:8 is among the most-cited verses in progressive religious advocacy, invariably in the form “do justice, love mercy” — and just as invariably without “walk humbly with thy God,” which is the clause that makes the other two possible and defines them. Micah is not proposing an ethical programme detachable from the God who shewed it; he is rebuking a nation that offered sacrifices instead of obedience. Justice defined by anything other than God's revealed law becomes whatever the strongest party calls justice. The Reformed reading keeps all three clauses and keeps them in order.
roots_summary: Hebrew tōb (good in every register — moral, aesthetic, useful, pleasant), the verdict word of Gen 1; Greek agathos (good in nature and effect) and kalos (good as beautiful and fit), which divide between them what Hebrew held in one.
roots_lines: tōb (Hebrew, H2896) — good, pleasant, agreeable, morally right; the verdict repeated seven times in Gen 1 and intensified at v. 31, and the word in “it is not good that the man should be alone.”
agathos (Greek, G18) — good in nature and in effect; the word in Rom 8:28 and in Eph 2:10, “created in Christ Jesus unto good works.”

kalos (Greek, G2570) — good as noble, beautiful, and fit to be seen; the word in Mat 5:16 (“that they may see your good works”) and in “the good shepherd” of Joh 10:11, where the shepherd is not merely effective but admirable.
summum bonum (Latin) — the highest good; the scholastic and Puritan term for God Himself as the creature's final blessedness, and the frame behind the Westminster Shorter Catechism's first answer.

1689 London Baptist Confession 16.1–3 — good works are only such as God hath commanded in His holy word, done in obedience to it, and wrought by the Spirit; the confessional guard against both moralism and antinomianism.
usage: Gen 1:31 is the church's standing answer to every form of Gnosticism: the material creation is not a fall from something purer but a thing God looked at and called very good.
Mar 10:18 is often misread as a disclaimer of deity. The logic runs the other way — the ruler is being asked whether he knows what he has just called Jesus, and the question is left standing.
The Hebrew tōb refuses the modern separation of the beautiful from the right. A Reformed aesthetic begins here: what is genuinely good is also, in its own order, fitting and lovely.
